analysis.one_liner: Bans consumer DNA testing companies from sharing Americans' genetic data with China or Chinese-controlled entities.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred DNA testing services from sending Americans' genetic information to China, never left committee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for commercial DNA testing services like ancestry and genealogy companies to disclose any American's genetic information — individual results or aggregated data — to the government of China or to any entity under China's influence, control, or ownership. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban the same way it enforces rules against unfair and deceptive business practices. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American who has taken a consumer DNA test — or ever might — would gain a legal guarantee that their genetic data cannot be handed to the Chinese government or to Chinese-owned or Chinese-controlled companies. Because genetic information is permanent, shared with relatives, and can reveal health risks, keeping it out of foreign government hands protects not only the customer but their family members.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans who use DNA testing services

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any commercial DNA testing service from disclosing an individual's genetic information, or aggregates of it, to the People's Republic of China or any entity under its influence, control, or ownership [S3].

It covers genealogical and ancestry-related services — the consumer DNA testing industry — and defines genetic information using the same definition as the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 [S3].
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban, treating a violation as an unfair or deceptive practice with the FTC Act's full penalty powers [S3].

The bill's stated subject area includes consumer affairs and the right of privacy, and it addresses growing concern that large collections of Americans' genetic data could be acquired by or shared with foreign governments [S1, S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer DNA testing companies would bear compliance costs and would lose the ability to monetize or share their genetic databases with Chinese buyers or partners. Any research or business partnerships involving aggregated genetic data and Chinese-controlled entities would be cut off. The cost to consumers is essentially none beyond whatever the companies pass on.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumer DNA and ancestry testing companies

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it bars disclosure to China only, not to Russia, Iran, data brokers generally, or any domestic purchaser, so most of the consumer genetic-data privacy problem — companies selling or sharing Americans' DNA data freely — remains untouched [S3].

The phrase 'under the influence, control, or ownership of' China is undefined in the bill text, which could create uncertainty for companies and researchers about what partnerships or data licenses are covered [S3].

Restrictions on sharing aggregate genetic data could complicate international scientific and biomedical research collaborations, a cost honest supporters of genetic privacy rules typically acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a legal bar on one of the most sensitive categories of personal data flowing to a foreign government — is real and costs consumers essentially nothing. But the bill is a narrow slice of the genetic privacy problem: it leaves DNA data free to move to other countries, to domestic data brokers, and to any buyer not tied to China. A broader genetic privacy bill would have protected far more; this one protects against one specific channel. The drawback that matters most is not the cost but the incompleteness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2025 [S1, S5].

narrative.text: Representative Tim Burchett, a Republican from Tennessee, introduced the bill on September 29, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1, S5].

On October 6, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce — the committee's subcommittee with jurisdiction over consumer data privacy — and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with six Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors, and it never advanced to a committee vote or the House floor [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer DNA testing companies are better off: they face no new FTC-enforced restrictions on where their genetic databases can go, and Chinese-controlled buyers retain access to a market the bill would have closed. Americans who took DNA tests remain without the protection the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: DNA testing companies and Chinese data buyers

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was entirely Republican — the sponsor plus six Republican cosponsors, no Democrats — but no one ever voted against it because it never reached a vote [S4].

industries.industry: Consumer DNA testing and genealogy companies
industries.note: The bill would have imposed an FTC-enforced ban on disclosing customer genetic data to China or Chinese-controlled entities, a real restriction on how these companies can monetize their databases. It would not have stopped domestic sales or transfers to other countries, so the industry's broader data business is left intact.

These entities would have been cut off from acquiring or licensing Americans' genetic data, including aggregated datasets that can reveal information about customers' relatives. Their interest in acquiring this data runs directly against the privacy interest of the Americans who provided it.
